note: Converted from the Tokyo AI City Travel Report (September 2026 edition), with travel context checked against GO TOKYO, the official Tokyo travel guide. Restaurant names and price bands are planning recommendations, not live availability: verify opening hours, reservation rules and prices before travel.

glance.why: Tokyo is one of the world's great cities of contrasts: a hyper-efficient megacity layered over the former Edo capital, where tiny neighborhood shrines, 400-year-old food traditions, cutting-edge design, anime, fashion, gardens and some of the world's most ambitious restaurants coexist within the same transit network. Its scale can feel overwhelming, but the best Tokyo experience comes from choosing a few districts and exploring them on foot between train rides. Tokyo is not improved by adding more pins to a map; the biggest mistake is trying to 'complete' it instead of choosing districts and spending time in them.
glance.idealStay: 4-5 days for a strong first visit; 3 days works if tightly curated; 7+ days for deeper neighborhoods, day trips and specialist interests
dontMiss: Tokyo Station, Marunouchi and the Imperial Palace area
One major museum or contemporary-art experience

history.story: Tokyo makes more sense when you understand that today's city is essentially several cities layered together. Edo began as a relatively small settlement, then changed dramatically when Tokugawa Ieyasu established the shogunate there in 1603. Over roughly 265 years of Tokugawa rule, peace, commerce, population growth and urban culture transformed Edo into one of the world's largest cities. In 1868, the Meiji Restoration ended the shogunate, Edo was renamed Tokyo, and the city became the imperial capital and a symbol of Japan's rapid modernization.
history.origins: Edo's position on the Kanto plain, its river and bay connections, and its role as the seat of Tokugawa power made it an ideal political and commercial center. Nihonbashi, established in 1603, became the starting point of the major highways radiating from Edo and remains a symbolic 'kilometer zero' of the city.

periods.name: Edo / Tokugawa era, 1603-1867
periods.text: The foundational period for Tokyo's urban culture, merchant districts, theater, food stalls, gardens, crafts and many enduring traditions.

periods.name: Meiji era, 1868-1912
periods.text: Edo becomes Tokyo and rapidly adopts railways, Western-style architecture, new institutions and industrial infrastructure.

periods.name: 20th century
periods.text: Tokyo experiences wartime destruction, postwar reconstruction and extraordinary economic growth, becoming a global business and cultural capital.

periods.name: Late 20th to 21st century
periods.text: The city continues to reinvent itself through high-density redevelopment, design, technology, pop culture, global dining and renewed interest in historic neighborhoods.

history.whyItMatters: Tokyo's history is visible rather than confined to museums. Asakusa preserves a traditional temple-and-shopping-street experience; Nihonbashi still reflects its historic commercial role; gardens such as Rikugien preserve Edo aesthetics; Ryogoku remains associated with sumo; and modern districts grew from different waves of railway, commercial and postwar development.
visible: Edo religion and entertainment, in Asakusa: Senso-ji, Nakamise, old-style shops and the former entertainment district
Edo commerce, in Nihonbashi: the historic bridge, department stores, traditional merchants and modern towers
Tokugawa power, around the Imperial Palace, Marunouchi and Ueno: the former castle core, gardens and Tokugawa-linked sites
Traditional urban life, in Yanaka and Nezu: low-rise streets, temples, small shops and surviving neighborhood texture
Performing arts, in Ginza at Kabukiza: kabuki as a living continuation of Tokyo's theatrical culture
Sumo culture, in Ryogoku: the Kokugikan area, chanko restaurants and sumo institutions

food.identity: Tokyo is less a single 'local cuisine' than Japan's greatest concentration point for regional ingredients, techniques and restaurant traditions. At the same time it has a distinct Edo/Tokyo food identity: Edomae sushi, soba, tempura, monjayaki, Fukagawa meshi and other dishes grew alongside the city's enormous Edo-period population and street-food culture. The practical takeaway is not to spend the trip chasing only famous sushi. Tokyo rewards variety: one high-quality sushi meal, one ramen lunch, soba or tempura, yakitori or izakaya, a neighborhood specialty and casual snacks give a much more complete picture. Spend less at lunch, make one reservation-worthy dinner count, and use another night for an izakaya or yokocho. Expensive does not mean better, and tipping is generally not expected, though some izakaya and bars apply a seating charge and bring a small dish before ordering.

practical.gettingAround: Use rail as the default: JR, Tokyo Metro, Toei Subway and private railways together reach almost every major visitor district, and the subway network alone has more than 280 stations with multilingual signage that makes it far easier than the map suggests. Get an IC card for frictionless travel - Welcome Suica and Tourist PASMO are the visitor-oriented options, and regular Suica or PASMO also work in many relevant areas. For a packed subway day, compare the cost of an IC card with the 24/48/72-hour Tokyo Subway Ticket, which covers Tokyo Metro and Toei Subway but not JR. Walking is not optional - it is part of the experience, and most neighborhoods are best understood by walking the 10-20 minutes between stations, shops and side streets. Taxis are useful late at night, with luggage, or when a group splits a fare, but are not necessary for ordinary sightseeing.
practical.whenToGo: Spring brings cherry blossoms and pleasant but crowded conditions - excellent, but book early. Early summer is green and warmer with a rainy season, and good for fewer crowds if rain is acceptable. Summer is hot and humid with festivals and fireworks; it is good for festivals but less comfortable for walking, so build in air-conditioned breaks and avoid scheduling every outdoor sight at midday. Autumn is mild with foliage and seasonal food, and is excellent overall. Winter is cool and dry with clear views and illuminations - excellent for city exploration and food, though daylight is shorter.

howLong.one: Asakusa, then Ueno or Tsukiji, then Ginza, then Shibuya or Shinjuku at night.
howLong.twoThree: Historic Tokyo plus Meiji Jingu, Harajuku and Shibuya, plus Tsukiji and Ginza, plus Shinjuku.
howLong.fourFive: Add a major museum, a slower neighborhood, deeper food experiences and one nature block or day trip.
howLong.week: Add multiple day trips, specialist shopping, craft and tea experiences, less-touristed districts and repeat visits to favorite food spots.

culture: Queue calmly and let passengers exit trains before boarding.
Keep phone conversations quiet on trains; eating and drinking on commuter trains is generally frowned upon.
Do not tip at ordinary restaurants.
At temples and shrines, observe the local sequence for washing, offerings and prayers; do not treat sacred spaces like photo sets.
At small bars and izakaya, check whether there is a cover or seating charge.
Cash is still useful for small independent businesses even though card and contactless acceptance is widespread.
Trash bins can be scarce; carry a small bag for your own waste.

Tsukiji Outer Market in the morning. Ginza, Nihonbashi and Tokyo Station in the afternoon. Shinjuku, Omoide Yokocho or Golden Gai in the evening.
